chapter_theme: The first half of Maduraikkanchi, Mangudi Maruthanar's counsel to the Pandya who won at Thalaiyalanganam: a long address that praises the king's lineage, battles, sieges, port wealth and giving, ravages his enemies' land, blesses him, and then sets against all this the countless kings who ruled as he does and passed away; with அதனால், 'therefore', it turns to a description of his realm in its five lands (marutham, mullai, kurinji, paalai, neythal) and approaches Madurai through the Vaiyai's banks, the refugees and defeated kings at its edge, its walls, its festival flags and its streets.
structure_note: The core cut placed most units in the middle of the poem's long participial sentences (break scores 0 and 1). Seventeen units were moved to the vocatives that close each address (lines 23, 42, 63, 74, 88, 105, 151, 176), to the start of the counsel (line 210), and to the 'ஒருசார்' and '... சான்ற' lines that close each of the five lands (270, 285, 301, 314, 326). The chapter ends at line 393 inside the description of the city, which continues in chapter 8.

pattupattu:6:1-23.reading: The poem opens on an ordered world, bounded by the roaring sea and standing on honey-hung mountains, where the winds keep their direction, the stars their course, sun and moon shine clear, the rain does its work, one seed yields a thousand and men are free of disease, and it names the king as descendant of the exalted ones who ruled that world among truthful, famous men, so that a good age followed in their steps.
pattupattu:6:1-23.nuance: The order of the cosmos is described before any king is named and is credited to the rule of the ancestors (lines 21 to 23); truthful speech (பொய் யறியா வாய்மொழி, line 19) is counted among the goods of that world alongside rain and harvest.
pattupattu:6:1-23.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 1-16 and 17-32: the opening sentence runs through the description of the ordered world (line 16 கட்கின் பத்து continues into line 17) to the vocative உயர்ந்தோர் மருக in line 23; line 24 begins the battlefield.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the patron through the ordered world his ancestors ruled

pattupattu:6:24-42.reading: On a dreadful field where elephants carry corpses on their tusks and demon women with fat in their mouths dance the tunangai in pairs, the blood of strong kings boils in the fire of wrath and, with a bangled arm for a ladle, the cook who knows the rite serves the flesh-rice to the soldiers who never stepped back; the king is hailed as lord of the hill of falling streams where the ancient god named after the southern king dwells.
pattupattu:6:24-42.nuance: The food of the rite goes to படை யோர் ... பிற் பெயரா, the soldiers who did not step back (lines 37, 38): the grisly sacrifice is also the army's reward. Lines 40 to 42 (தென்னவற் பெயரிய ... தொல்முது கடவுள்) are hard: the hill may be one where an ancient god bearing the Pandya's name dwells, or the king may be said to dwell after that god; the reading is not fixed.
pattupattu:6:24-42.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 17-32 and 33-42: the battlefield passage begins at பிணக் கோட்ட in line 24 and closes with the vocative பொருப்பிற் பொருந in line 42.

thinai_evidence.note: the battlefield sacrifice after victory, a deed of vaakai

comparisons.tenor: the wrath of the strong kings, as the fire on which their own blood boils

pattupattu:6:43-63.reading: While the great war-trained elephant, mountain-like, its head wet with fragrant musth, tramples the field in fury, the dust the horses raise hides the sun, the swift chariots whirl like wind and sword-bearing warriors fight shoulder to shoulder, the king defeats the two great kings together with the Velir, crosses falling hills and splits the wilderness, and, descendant of the golden-garlanded Nediyon who gave the land, is like the white thunderbolt that eats trees and shatters mountains.
pattupattu:6:43-63.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 43-56 and 57-72: the sentence of the battle and the lineage closes at ஏற னையை, 'you are like the thunderbolt', in line 63; line 64 begins the forts.

thinai_evidence.note: victory over the two crowned kings and the Velir

comparisons.tenor: the war elephant's towering height
the speed of the chariots wheeling on the field
the king's destroying force

pattupattu:6:64-74.reading: Going on without pause he took, and left, forts with guard forests, deep moats, rows of tall gates, long walls with lines of battlements and arrow-spitting towers, so that from southern Kumari to the great northern mountain and between the eastern and western seas the kings who lived in victory speak their old allegiance and obey, and he will be king over them all.
pattupattu:6:64-74.nuance: The bounds of rule in lines 70 and 71 (Kumari, the northern mountain, the two seas) are the formula Purananuru 6 and 17 also use; here they come as the result of a run of sieges, not as an inheritance.
pattupattu:6:64-74.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 57-72 and 73-82: the sieges begin at அருங் குழுமிளை in line 64 and the sentence ends in கோனா குவை, 'you will be king of kings', line 74.

thinai_evidence.note: the taking of fortified strongholds, a deed of uzhinai

pattupattu:6:75-88.reading: On the dread, sky-touching sea, ships with sails raised on tall masts cut the curling waves before a strong wind and come to shore to the sound of drums, unloading gold and precious goods that fill the land, great rocking ships like cloud-capped mountains crowding the harbour; the king is hailed as the lofty victor who took that town of tall paddy with the clear sea for its moat.
pattupattu:6:75-88.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 73-82 and 83-105: the sea passage that begins at வானி யைந்த in line 75 closes with the vocative உயர் கொற்றவ in line 88.

thinai_evidence.note: the capture of a sea-moated town, whose port wealth is the praise

comparisons.tenor: the great ships crowding the harbour

pattupattu:6:89-105.reading: Everywhere sound the songs of the water-lifters at their rows of lifts, the clear bells of the threshers' oxen that scare off the great birds, and the kuravai of the fisherwomen on the sandy shore of blue-flowered mundakam, while on one side, in the wide festival ground, the king gives the drum-shouldered bards bright-tusked elephants, crowns them with golden lotuses and scatters fine ornaments: he is the victorious king of the many Kuttuvar.
pattupattu:6:89-105.nuance: The giving is set among the sounds of field and shore (இசையே என்றும், line 95): the bards' gift belongs to the same abundance as the threshing and the fisherwomen's dance. Line 92 கய னகைய and line 101 இரு பெயர்ப் பேரா யம் are obscure.
pattupattu:6:89-105.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 83-105: the sounds of the fields and the shore begin at நீர்த் தெவ்வும் in line 89 and lead to the gifts and the vocative வெல் கோவே, line 105.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving to the bards amid the sounds of his land

comparisons.tenor: the bards' broad, rounded shoulders

pattupattu:6:106-130.reading: Even when summer scorches the stones, the sky hides its rain and the stars of the coming days go astray, the king's land never lacks flood or harvest: the din of paddy and reapers and the cries of birds never cease, and on the shore the fishermen landing their boats and the sellers of white salt keep up the noise of Muthuvellil's wealth; with the farmers of the small hamlets and the people of the four lands obeying him, he swept on like wind, spread fire till the land was ruined, camped fearsomely at Alankanam, crushed the kings, took their drums and made the battlefield his sacrifice.
pattupattu:6:106-130.nuance: Lines 106 to 109 claim that the land yields even when rain fails and the stars go wrong, the reverse of the rule that rain follows the king; the land's plenty is offered as given, and the counsel that comes later has to work on a king who has it.

thinai_evidence.note: the victory at Alankanam closes the unit

comparisons.tenor: the screwpine with its drum-like fruit
the king's swift onset

pattupattu:6:131-151.reading: He raises the houses of his friends and unseats the kingdoms of his foes; desired by the people of good Korkai with its ripe pearls and conch-bangled quarters, he is the war-bull of the southern fisherfolk who eat rich meat; taking everything hard with ease and throwing away all that is his without keeping it, he will not say 'let us stay' but rises, goes through the forests of the snowy peaks, enters the inner lands, seizes what they prize and camps for many years in the land he wants.
pattupattu:6:131-151.nuance: Lines 131 and 132 (நட்டவர் குடி யுயர்க் குவை, செற்றவர் அரசு பெயர்க் குவை) set friend and foe in one balanced pair; lines 145 and 146 pair taking and giving away the same way.
pattupattu:6:131-151.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 131-144 and 145-160: the address that begins at நட்டவர் குடி in line 131 runs through the vocative போ ரேறே (144) to வெல்போர்க் குருசில் in line 151; line 152 turns to the enemy's land.

thinai_evidence.note: setting out and camping for years in the enemy's land

comparisons.tenor: the king as leader of the southern fisherfolk in war

pattupattu:6:152-176.reading: In the land of the enemies he entered, the guarded groves are cut down, fire grazes the great fields that never knew want, what was called country becomes forest, wild beasts stand where cattle stood and waste where towns stood; the young women forget the tunangai, demon women sing in the halls where assemblies sat, grieving women cry at the gates, families scatter to others' shelter, the crested owl hoots with its mate in fallen mansions, sedge and reed choke the lily pond and the boar frisks with his sow in the ploughed fields: for lack of living, his enemies' land has become a ruin.
pattupattu:6:152-176.nuance: Each human use of the land is replaced by a wild one in a paired line (cattle by beasts, town by waste, dance by demon song, the ploughed field by the boar and sow); the owl calling to its mate (குராலொடு, line 170) and the boar with its sow put animal couples where the families were.
pattupattu:6:152-176.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 145-160 and 161-176: the devastation begins at உறு செறுநர் புலம் புக்கவர் in line 152 and closes at பாழா யினநின் பகைவர் தேஎம், line 176.

thinai_evidence.note: the ravaging of the enemy's land after the invasion

pattupattu:6:177-198.reading: Spreading fierce tall-tusked elephants and an army wide as the sea, going against his foes like Murugan, arrows falling like rain, horses raising dust and conches and horns sounding, he broke their pride, took their forts and rooted them out with their kin, so that his enemies walk his way; he has ringed the old wide world, shown the path of dharma without failing in statecraft or straying from the steps of the great, and the poet wishes his victory to grow like the waxing crescent seen in the west and his foes' fortune to wane like the moon rising in the east; even for heaven with its nectar he would not leave his true friendship for a lie.
pattupattu:6:177-198.nuance: The two moon similes of lines 193 to 196 are exactly matched: the crescent first seen in the west waxes, the moon that rises in the east after full moon wanes, so the king's growth and his enemies' decline are one cycle seen from two sides. Line 198 turns praise into a standard: a friendship free of lies.

thinai_evidence.note: the unit ends in blessing and praise of conduct; the battle is the ground of the praise

comparisons.tenor: the king going against his enemies
the arrows he scatters
the extent of his army
the growth of the king's victory, generation after generation
the waning of his enemies' fortune

pattupattu:6:199-209.reading: Even if the great ones of the high world came offering the earth ringed by the roaring sea, he would not bow and walk in fear of his enemies; even if he could have the treasure Vanan buried to fill the southern land, he would not say 'let blame come to us', but seeks fame with a mind to give treasure away; and now the poet asks leave to say one thing: let the lord of slaying war listen, may his sorrow perish and his far-shining fame stand unperishing.
pattupattu:6:199-209.nuance: With கொன்னொன்று கிளக்குவல் ... கேட்டிசின் (lines 207, 208) the poet stops praising and announces counsel: the kaanchi of the colophon begins here. The praise of lines 199 to 205 is phrased in the conditional (வரினும், பெறினும்), as tests the king is said to pass.
pattupattu:6:199-209.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 199-214 and 215-237: the praise of the king's integrity and the poet's call to listen close with நல்லிசை in line 209; the counsel begins at தவாப் பெருக்கத்து in line 210 and runs as one sentence to line 237.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's integrity, leading to the poet's call to listen

pattupattu:6:210-237.reading: The kings of many spears who had sacred cities of unfailing plenty, meat and rice and sharp liquor that never ran short however much was taken, treasure the ground could not hold; who filled the viralis' empty hands with bangles, gave the bards elephants and the panegyrists chariots and horses, drank toddy among great men, made the bowed lands follow them and set up camp over which no kite could fly to take tribute from the unbowed: those kings, more than the sand the waves throw on the shore, ruled the wide world with their fame spreading, and passed away.
pattupattu:6:210-237.nuance: Every mark of greatness the poem has praised in its own king so far (plenty, giving to bards, conquest, tribute) is here given to the dead kings before him; the sentence is one long relative clause that ends only on கழிந்தோரே, so the reader learns that these were all past kings at the last word.
pattupattu:6:210-237.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 199-214 and 215-237: the sentence that begins at தவாப் பெருக்கத்து in line 210 runs to ஆண்டுகழிந் தோரே in line 237 (line 214 ends inside the word வைகல்).

thinai_evidence.note: the many great kings who ruled and are gone: counsel of impermanence

comparisons.tenor: the number of kings who ruled and passed

pattupattu:6:238-260.reading: Therefore: the clouds, drawing from the eastern sea and closing on the western, pour day and night without pause till falls roar in the rocky clefts and the elephant herds tremble on the bamboo slopes, and the flood that the land cannot hold runs back toward the eastern sea and fills the tanks; in fields where the grain hides elephants and in pools of lotus, neythal, blue lily and aambal, the fishermen disturb the waterhen's sleep scooping fish from the vallai, and the reed fields ring with the cane press, the weeders and the shouts of toddy-drunk field hands hauling oxen out of the mire.
pattupattu:6:238-260.nuance: அதனால், 'therefore', at line 238 ties the long description of the five lands to the counsel just given about the kings who passed: the description is the ground of an argument whose conclusion lies beyond this chapter. The rain starts on the hills (kurinji things) and ends in the fields, so the marutham section is built as the journey of the water.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the marutham fields of the king's land

pattupattu:6:261-270.reading: In fields where pakanrai spreads and the grain is ripe, the reapers' drum sounds sweetly, and from cool Parankunram, where soft rain falls, comes the noise of the crowd of men and women who play together in dense garlands and wreaths; all these sounds ring sweetly in the wide sky, with the herons' cries and the bards' quarter where fish are scaled by the house trees, around the cool fields of the marutham land.
pattupattu:6:261-270.nuance: The hill festival at Parankunram is counted as one more sound of the marutham countryside, between the reaping drum and the herons; the bards here (பாண் சேரி) scale fish, a reminder that the Paanar were also a fishing people.
pattupattu:6:261-270.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 238-260 and 261-279: the marutham section closes at மருதஞ் சான்ற தண்பணை சுற்றி ஒருசார், line 270; line 271 begins the mullai section.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the marutham land, closing its section

pattupattu:6:271-285.reading: On one side, as the small millet is cut, the pulse darkens and the dark-stalked varagu's ears dry, gems glitter in deep pits and gold is sifted in the woods, small-headed stags frisk with their soft-eyed does, kondrai petals strew the shade over rocks spread like mats, silver-white blossoms fall on crops green as sapphire, musundai and mullai spread, and flowers rivalling the gem-blue neythal open in the clear hollows with thoyyil: like a veri ground laid out by a skilled hand, the forest country full of mullai is adorned.
pattupattu:6:271-285.nuance: The closing simile (line 284) likens the whole flowering forest to a veri ground laid out for Murugan's rite, so the mullai section ends on a kurinji rite; the stag with his doe (lines 275, 276) is scene here, in a puram description with no lovers.
pattupattu:6:271-285.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 261-279 and 280-292: the mullai section runs from சிறுதினை கொய்ய, line 271, to முல்லை சான்ற புறவணிந் தொருசார், line 285.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the mullai land of the realm

comparisons.tenor: the broad flat rocks
the green of the crops
the white blossoms falling
the blue flowers of the forest hollows
the forest strewn with flowers

pattupattu:6:286-301.reading: On one side, where fragrant hardwood has been felled and sown with digging sticks, short-eared thorai paddy, tall mustard and white aivanam rice grow thick with ginger, turmeric, green pepper and many other goods gathered among the rocks, and the shouts of the parrot-scarers on the millet slopes, of the hunters driving wild cattle off the avarai shoots, at the boar fallen into the watchman's pit, of those plucking vengai flowers and at the tiger that killed a bull all gather with the white falls on the slopes: the hills full of kurinji are adorned, embracing the great guarded mountain.
pattupattu:6:286-301.nuance: The section is built from five பூசல், 'shouts' (lines 291 to 298), each the noise of one hill occupation, so the kurinji land, like the marutham, is given by its sounds.
pattupattu:6:286-301.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 280-292 and 293-308: the kurinji section runs from நறுங்காழ் கொன்று, line 286, to அருங்கடி மாமலை தழீஇ ஒருசார், line 301.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the kurinji land of the realm

pattupattu:6:302-314.reading: On one side, where sharp fire wastes the green clumps of great bamboo, lean elephants go off to graze, the bamboo bursts at its nodes with a crackle like musicians striking their drums and loses its beauty, the great hill stands bare with its falls dried up, the dry grass is like straw and the west wind scoops the clefts with a roar like the wind-driven sea, harsh-voiced young men in garlands of withered leaves, bows in hand, guard the forking paths from their leaf huts with deer-skin beds: the wilderness full of paalai lies among the summer hills that have lost their shade.
pattupattu:6:302-314.nuance: The paalai has no land of its own: it is the hill country gone dry (அருவி யான்ற, நிழலுரு விழந்த), which is how porul 1.11 describes it, and the poem says so by placing it in 'summer hills'.
pattupattu:6:302-314.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 293-308 and 309-323: the paalai section runs from இருவெதிர்ப் பைந்தூறு, line 302, to பாலை சான்ற சுரஞ்சேர்ந் தொருசார், line 314.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the realm through its paalai wilderness

comparisons.tenor: the crackle of the bamboo bursting in the fire
the dry grass of the burnt forest
the roar of the wind in the clefts

pattupattu:6:315-326.reading: On one side, bright pearls the roaring sea yields, shining bangles sawn from conch, the many grains the traders bring, sweet tamarind and white salt from the pans of the great backwater, slices of fat fish cut by the strong-handed boatmen, and the horses brought together by those who sail great ships to fetch fine goods from distant lands, all grow day by day as the many riches of the neythal gather, and so the lands of all five kinds flourish and are settled.
pattupattu:6:315-326.nuance: Line 326 names the scheme the description has followed: ஐம்பால் திணை, the land of five kinds, each introduced by '... சான்ற' and 'ஒருசார்'; the neythal is given not by its sounds, as the others are, but by its goods, most of them traded.
pattupattu:6:315-326.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 309-323 and 324-340: the neythal section runs from முழங்குகடல் தந்த, line 315, to the line that closes all five lands, ஐம்பால் திணையுங் கவினி யமைவர, line 326.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the neythal wealth, closing the description of all five lands

comparisons.tenor: the round slices of fish

pattupattu:6:327-342.reading: In the middle of that land rich in song, with its wide drum-beating grounds, its festival streets and its quarters fragrant with weddings where the tunangai is danced and joyful crowds gather, along every bank of the Vaiyai, where stags roam the high peaks, peacocks call in the groves, monkeys play, wind-struck trees rise to the sky and the flowing water heaps white sand, the pollen-laden kongu strews its flowers and the river flows like a garland; and at every ford, surrounded by gardens of many flowers, are the long-settled quarters of the great bards.
pattupattu:6:327-342.unit_note: Adjusted from the core units 324-340 and 341-361: the description of the festive streets and the Vaiyai's banks begins at முழ வீமிழும், line 327, and the sentence closes on the bards' settlement, பெரும்பாண் இருக்கையும், line 342; line 343 turns to the dispossessed.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the land around Madurai and the river

comparisons.tenor: the river flowing with flowers on it

pattupattu:6:343-361.reading: There too are those who lost lands as rich as Azhumbil of the proud victorious Vel, whose land and wealth no eye could take in, and those who lost their rich new homes, and the kings of lordly elephants who came in old enmity and fled, leaving their drums in the middle ground; then the city: a moat of clear water sunk deep, a many-layered rampart rising to the sky, a tall gateway with its guardian goddess and doors blackened with poured ghee, mansions like cloud-capped mountains, a gate as busy as the Vaiyai, many-windowed houses singing in the breeze, and long wide streets lying like a river, where the voices of many crowds rise like the sea lifted by a great wind.
pattupattu:6:343-361.nuance: The city is approached through its refugees: those who lost lands and homes, and the defeated kings, stand at its edge before the moat and walls are described, so the king's capital is shown to be fed by his wars. The sense of கண்டமை கல்லா (line 343) is not certain.
pattupattu:6:343-361.unit_note: Adjusted from the core unit 341-361: the list of the dispossessed begins at நிலனும் வளனுங் in line 343 (lines 341 and 342 close the description of the Vaiyai's banks), and the unit still ends at the crowd simile of line 361.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the city through those it has displaced and its defences

comparisons.tenor: the lands the dispossessed have lost
the height of the mansions
the flow of traffic through the gate
the long wide streets
the din of the crowds in the streets

pattupattu:6:362-379.reading: Drummers proclaim the news on the loud drum, instruments ring like hands splashing a pool, the joyful dance makes a din, and over the two great markets, like a painting, stand the many figured flags of the festival, the flags raised each time a strong fort was taken, the flags of fame raised by those who routed the shield-ranks with an army of spears that roars like water, the flags of the toddy shops and many crowd banners and pennants, waving like falls on a great mountain side; like a ship in a deep whirlpool of the wide sea, its ropes snapped, sail torn, mast shattered by the fierce wind and dashed on the rocks...
pattupattu:6:362-379.nuance: The flags are sorted by what they record (festival, each fort taken, a victory, the toddy shop), so the skyline of the market is a record of the king's wars; the ship simile that ends the unit is completed only by the elephant of line 383.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the city's festival and the flags of its victories

comparisons.tenor: the sound of the struck instruments
the two great markets
the roar of the spear army
the waving of the flags
the musth elephant that breaks loose (line 383, in the next unit)

pattupattu:6:380-393.reading: With the two-headed conch sounding, the musth elephant in rage kills its goad-men, throws off its riders, ignores soft bonds and strong chains, bends its post and leaves its pillar to roam; the beautiful chariot runs fast as wind with horses of bright manes like the red-legged swan cock that cleaves the wind toward the sun; horses with plumed crests, trained in circling paces by the whip-holding rider, go by; and toddy-drunk field hands, fearsome in their going like elephants, brawl in a great tangle.
pattupattu:6:380-393.nuance: Elephant, chariot and horse are the limbs of an army, but here they move through festival streets, and the fourth limb, the foot soldiers, is replaced by drunken field hands; களமர் may also be read as warriors, which would make the last line a mock battle. In line 386 அன்னத்து is the swan, not the particle.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the city through the elephants, chariots and horses of its streets

comparisons.tenor: the bright-maned chariot horses
the speed of the chariot
the fearsome going of the drunken field hands

links.note: The Kural says rain and harvest gather in the land of the king who rules by right; the idyll opens on a world where the rain does its work, one seed yields a thousand and men are free of disease, and credits it to the rule of the patron's ancestors among truthful men.
links.teaches: The idyll gives the Kural's cause-and-effect rule a cosmic setting and a past: the plenty is the order of the world itself and belongs to the ancestors' rule, so a king inherits a moral weather he must keep up rather than earning it afresh, which is what the counsel later in the poem asks of him.

links.note: The same poet praises the same king for the battlefield sacrifice: in Purananuru 26 with crowned heads for a hearth, blood for water and bangled arms for ladles; in the idyll with the arm as ladle and the flesh-rice served to the soldiers who did not step back.
links.teaches: Mangudi Maruthanar's two accounts of the rite show what it was for: the short poem sets it beside the king's Vedic sacrifices as a second, martial sacrifice, while the idyll names who eats it, the soldiers who held their ground, so the horror is also the army's feast and reward.

links.note: The idyll gives the victory at Alankanam as its patron's crowning deed (camping fearsomely, killing kings, taking their drums); in Akananuru 209 the friend says the gossip about the heroine is louder than the roar at Alankanam when Chezhiyan beat the seven.
links.teaches: Held together, the two show the battle the court poet offers as the king's defining glory already serving an akam poet as a proverbial measure of noise for village gossip, so a royal victory entered the common stock of comparison and was expected to be known to every hearer.

links.note: Kalladanar tells the same king that he has seen the ruin of the enemy's land, ending on a doe with her fawn, her stag killed by a tiger, nibbling velai flowers in a manless waste; the idyll lists, line by line, each human use of the enemy's land replaced by a wild one, with the owl and its mate in the fallen mansions and the boar and its sow in the ploughed fields.
links.teaches: Both poets of this king measure conquest by animal couples moving into places emptied of human families, so the ravaged-land description had a fixed device; the idyll turns Kalladanar's single pathetic image into a systematic inversion of the land's uses, which is the material its kaanchi counsel will later weigh.

links.note: Purananuru 182 says the world endures because some would not eat even Indra's nectar alone; the idyll says the king would not leave true friendship for a lie even if he gained the high world with its nectar.
links.teaches: The 'even for the gods' nectar' test appears in both, but Purananuru 182 uses it for sharing among anonymous worthies while the idyll uses it for a king's truthfulness to his friends, so the virtues that hold the world together were also demanded of the ruler, and the measure for them was the same.

links.note: The Kural rates the worst poverty of the worthy above wealth won under blame; the idyll says the king, offered the treasure Vanan buried in the south, would not say 'let blame come to us', but would rather give treasure away for fame.
links.teaches: The idyll shows the Kural's maxim as a king's test with a named treasure and adds the alternative the Kural leaves out, giving wealth away for fame, so refusing blamed gain is tied to giving: the ruler's honour lies in both refusing and spending.

links.note: Mangudi Kizhar ends Purananuru 24 by saying that the only ones who truly lived are those who, born in the wide world, did not pass with the many but stayed in fame; in the idyll he says the kings who ruled the wide world with their fame spreading are more than the sand on the shore, and are gone.
links.teaches: The same poet who told this king that fame alone outlasts death here counts the famous kings by the grains of sand, so fame does not exempt anyone from passing and is itself common; the counsel of the idyll is harder than the short poem's consolation, and the pair shows the kaanchi argument being sharpened by its own author.

links.note: The idyll counts the noise of the garlanded crowd playing together on cool Parankunram among the sounds of the marutham countryside; Paripadal 17 describes the crowds revelling between song-rich Koodal and Parankunram, garlanded men and women dancing so that the bees cannot reach the flowers.
links.teaches: In the Maduraikkanchi the Parankunram festival is one sound among the reaping drum and the herons, part of the king's agrarian land, while the Paripadal makes the same crowd its subject and the hill's beauty, so the festival a court poet counted as rural plenty became, in the devotional songs, the sign of the god's hill.

source_issues: The idyll's colophon has no thurai (the record gives only the thinai காஞ்சி); puram_thurai is therefore empty for every unit.
Line 112 கறவுக் is obscure; சுறவுக் (shark) would fit புலவு நீர் வியன் பெளவத்து in the next line and may be the intended reading.
Line 187 நா டழியக் எயில் has an irregular doubled க் before a vowel (expected நாடழிய எயில்).
Line 214 ends inside a word: தின் றானா இன வைக / னிலனெடுக் (lines 214, 215) splits வைகல் and நிலன் across the line break as printed.
Line 308 கமழ்சூழ் is flagged against the tamilvu reading கமஞ்சூழ் (full, laden); our reading is kept, and the karu and mutal of that unit do not depend on it.

Line 323 புரவிய டனைத்தும் looks like the same loss of the vowel sign ொ that was repaired at lines 172, 180, 269, 276, 281, 299, 369 and 372 (புரவியொடு அனைத்தும்); it is not flagged and the karu form is copied as printed.
